title: Shifting the Gradient: Understanding How Defensive Training Methods Protect Language Model Integrity
claim: Both defensive training methods shift the training signal from amplifying to attenuating along the trait axis, though the size of that shift doesn't track defensive strength.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: schematic, dumbbell plot, dumbbell plot with shared rows
description: Three panels. Panel (a) is a schematic with two stacked 3-axis sketches. The top one, 'no defense', shows a gray arrow along a 'persona axis' and a faint dashed arrow labeled ⟨−∂L/∂h, v⟩ pointing forward. The bottom one, 'PPS', adds a purple +εv segment, and its dashed gradient arrow points backward. Panel (b) is a dumbbell plot of mean cosine C̄ at the steering layer. Rows are six traits on Qwen2.5-7B and three other models. Gray squares mark no defense, purple circles mark PPS, and green diamonds mark IP. A gray shaded region labeled 'attenuating' sits left of zero, with 'amplifying' on the right. Panel (c) shows trait expression on a 0–100 scale for the same rows, with a black tick marking the base model. A legend box sits at bottom left.
caption: PPS and IP shift the training signal along the trait axis. (a) Schematic of the gradient shift: the activation's component along the "evil" persona vector (PV) $v$, $\langle h, v\rangle$, and the training signal on it, $\langle -\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h, v\rangle$. Without defense, training on "evil" data pushes the activation further along the PV; adding the PPS vector $\epsilon v$ to the forward pass reverses the push. (b) The measured shift in six traits on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and for "evil" on three other models: $\bar C$, the cosine between $-\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h$ and each setting's own PV at its steering layer, with no defense (grey squares), PPS (purple circles) and IP (green diamonds), at the nearest available calibration match where applicable; pirate, all-caps and optimism use fallback defaults (Appx. [ref]). PPS shifts the gradient to attenuating (shaded) in every setting, and further than IP. (c) Trait expression after finetuning in the same settings. Both defenses reduce expression, but the size of the gradient shift along the PV axis does not order their defensive strength (Section [ref]).
abstract: Defensive training methods such as positive preventative steering (PPS) and inoculation prompting (IP) offer surprising results through seemingly similar processes: both add trait-inducing objects to large language models (LLMs) during training, and both defend the LLM against acquiring the trait. The success of these methods raises the questions: how do they work, and are they doing the same thing? We provide behavioral and mechanistic analyses of PPS and IP, using the acquisition of an ``evil'' persona by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as an in-depth case study and replicating key measurements across six traits and four models. Behaviorally, neither method operates through a purely associative mechanism, and both methods prevent trait acquisition; but PPS can also substantially reduce pre-existing trait expression, whereas IP does so only modestly. Mechanistically, PPS induces a concentrated change in the activation gradient and shifts the signal along the trait direction from amplifying to attenuating, whereas IP changes the gradient more diffusely and shifts it close to zero along the trait direction. Gradient manipulations show that the direction of this component is causally relevant to trait acquisition, although it is one effect rather than a complete account of either defense. We then show that IP lowers the next-token prediction loss on trait-expressing data, whereas PPS can raise it at the intensities at which it defends; we show how this analysis raises the possibility that the loss changes and the gradient shift are two summaries of the same training signal rather than completely separate mechanisms. Together, our results show that PPS and IP are not interchangeable, and they highlight open questions about a complete mechanistic picture.
